questions.prompt: A discrete-time system is stable when all poles are
questions.explanation: In the z-plane, the stability boundary is the unit circle, not the imaginary axis. Poles inside \(|z| < 1\) decay. Poles on the unit circle give sustained oscillation. Poles outside grow without bound.

questions.prompt: A first-order discrete system has pole at \(z = 0.8\). The equivalent continuous-time pole, if the sample time is \(T = 0.1\) s, is at
questions.explanation: The mapping is \(z = e^{sT}\), so \(s = \ln(z)/T = \ln(0.8)/0.1 = -2.23\). The pole is in the left half-plane, corresponding to a decaying mode.

questions.figure_alt: The z-plane with the unit circle.

questions.prompt: Same pole at \(z = 0.8\), sample time 0.1 s. The time constant of the discrete mode is
questions.explanation: The continuous pole is \(s = \ln(0.8)/0.1 = -2.23\). The time constant is \(1/|-2.23| = 0.45\) s. This is how long the mode takes to decay by \(e^{-1}\).

questions.figure_alt: The z-plane with the unit circle.

questions.prompt: The z-transform maps a continuous-time pole at \(s = -a\) with sample time \(T\) to
questions.explanation: The exact discretization gives \(z = e^{sT}\). For \(s = -a\), that is \(z = e^{-aT}\). The pole moves inside the unit circle if \(a > 0\). The other options are not the correct mapping.

questions.prompt: A continuous pole at \(s = -2\) with sample time \(T = 0.5\) s maps to \(z =\)
questions.explanation: \(z = e^{-2 \times 0.5} = e^{-1} = 0.368\). The pole is well inside the unit circle, indicating a fast decay relative to the sample rate.

options: the signal frequency exceeds half the sample rate
the pole is inside the unit circle
the sample rate is too high
questions.explanation: Nyquist's theorem requires sampling at more than twice the signal frequency. Frequencies above half the sample rate (the Nyquist frequency) fold back as aliases. This is a sampling limitation, not a stability issue.

questions.prompt: A first-order plant \(G(s) = 1/(s+1)\) is sampled at \(T = 0.2\) s. The discrete pole is at \(z =\)
questions.explanation: The continuous pole is at \(s = -1\). Discretized, \(z = e^{-1 \times 0.2} = e^{-0.2} = 0.819\). This is a standard zero-order hold discretization.

questions.prompt: A discrete system has poles at \(z = 0.6 \pm 0.5j\). The magnitude is
questions.explanation: \(|z| = \sqrt{0.36 + 0.25} = 0.78\). Since \(|z| < 1\), the system is stable. The poles are a conjugate pair giving an oscillatory but decaying response.

options: has no effect on pole location
questions.explanation: As \(T \to 0\), \(z = e^{sT} \to 1\) for any finite \(s\). Faster sampling means the pole is closer to \(z = 1\), which represents a slower decay per sample. Numerical issues can arise when \(T\) is too small.

questions.prompt: A sampled-data system has sample time 0.05 s. The Nyquist frequency is
questions.explanation: The Nyquist frequency is half the sample rate: \(f_N = 1/(2T) = 10\) Hz. Signals above 10 Hz will alias. In rad/s, the Nyquist rate is \(2\pi \times 10 = 62.8\) rad/s.

questions.prompt: A digital controller has a computational delay of one sample. In the z-domain, this delay is represented by
questions.explanation: One sample delay multiplies the transfer function by \(z^{-1}\). This shifts the output by one sample. Multiple delays give \(z^{-n}\). The continuous delay \(e^{-sT}\) is the time-domain equivalent.

questions.prompt: A rule of thumb: sample at least 10 times per time constant. For a plant with \(\tau = 0.5\) s, the maximum sample period is
questions.explanation: The sample period should be \(T \le \tau/10 = 0.5/10 = 0.05\) s. This ensures the discrete controller captures the plant dynamics. Sampling too slowly loses information.
